Daniel’s line is sharp because it exposes a common category mistake: “free will doesn’t exist” is (at best) a metaphysical claim about how actions are caused, while “what should you do?” is a normative question about reasons, values, and social practices. Even if libertarian free will were false, deliberation doesn’t evaporate—it becomes one of the causal processes through which future behavior is shaped. In that sense, the right follow-up isn’t “so nothing matters,” but “given that beliefs and incentives change actions, which deliberative habits and institutions make better lives more likely?” This is close to the pragmatist/compatibilist move in [Daniel Dennett’s *Elbow Room*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbow_Room_(Dennett_book)): treat “free will” less as a spooky power and more as the cluster of capacities (foresight, self-control, responsiveness to reasons) that practical guidance actually targets.

A hidden assumption Daniel might make more explicit is that the “should” here is intelligible without specifying a moral framework. Different ethical theories answer “what should you do with your will?” differently—virtue ethics points to character formation, consequentialism to outcomes, deontology to duties—and none of them strictly requires metaphysical indeterminism. What the free-will debate *does* threaten, if mishandled, is responsibility talk: people slide from determinism to fatalism (“I can’t do otherwise, so why try?”), or from metaphysical skepticism to moral skepticism (“no one deserves anything”). That slide is precisely what [P.F. Strawson’s “Freedom and Resentment”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_and_Resentment) tries to block by arguing that our responsibility practices are rooted in interpersonal life, not in settling causal metaphysics. If Daniel wants the thought to land harder, he could say so plainly: denying free will doesn’t answer “what should I do?” because it doesn’t even *try* to answer “what is worth wanting?” or “which forms of accountability improve human behavior?”—and those are the questions people are usually reaching for.
